description: We're a team of six students from Takoradi taking part in NASA Space Apps 2026. We enjoy building practical software with data, machine learning and AI, and we want to use NASA data to solve a real problem over the weekend. Our strengths are software development, data analysis and machine learning, and we're aiming to build a working prototype with a clear demo.

details:
CrewCare is an offline-first health companion that helps astronauts check their own health and know what to do next when Earth cannot answer quickly. It was built by Team Lunar in Takoradi for the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts challenge. On the International Space Station, a flight surgeon is always reachable and evacuation is possible. On a Mars mission, a message takes about twenty-two minutes each way, there is no evacuation and there is no resupply. CrewCare is designed for that gap: a tool the crew itself can use, alone, with no connection.

The app opens on a dashboard for the whole crew. Each astronaut has a green, amber or red badge, with an arrow showing whether their health is rising, falling or steady. Tapping a person opens their own thirty-day picture: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood, each charted against that person's own pre-flight baseline over thirty days, rather than against a population average. Radiation exposure and eye changes are tracked alongside the daily readings, because both are known spaceflight risks. New readings are entered by hand through check-in, and the app explains how to take each measurement and why it matters.

When something feels wrong, guided triage walks a non-doctor through four questions: is the person responsive, breathing, and do they have a pulse or chest pain? The answers lead to a red or amber outcome with concrete steps under do now, check next, prepare, and tell Earth. Triage never names a disease. The on-board crew medical officer acts at once; the message to Earth is for guidance, never something the crew waits for. The app also keeps a medical inventory, so the crew can see what is available before they act.

CrewCare works fully offline after its first load. A service worker saves every file of the app on the device on the first visit, then serves the app from that saved copy when there is no connection. Readings, the message outbox and the mission environment are stored on the device itself and never leave it. Messages use store and forward: a message is saved as pending, waits out the communication delay for the environment, then flips to sent. The demo shortens the Mars delay to thirty seconds and labels it as a demo; the real delay is about twenty-two minutes each way. If the app closes while a message is waiting, nothing is lost.

The design is grounded in NASA data as its core evidence. The check-in fields follow the NASA Human Research Program Standard Measures, and the evidence panels draw on the five hazards of human spaceflight and on Open Science Data Repository study OSD-816 on spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome and eyes. Sleep evidence comes from published bed-rest research (AGBRESA). A Canadian Space Agency article on radiation, about one millisievert per day on the International Space Station, is used as context. The crew readings in the app are simulated data created by the team for demonstration, not NASA data.

Existing systems leave the gap CrewCare fills. Health checks on the station today are periodic, using a blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter, thermometer, blood analyser and ultrasound, with a flight surgeon on the ground at all times. The Canadian Bio-Monitor smart shirt records vital signs continuously, but sends its data to scientists on the ground. The Oura Ring was tested for sleep on Axiom Mission 4, processing data on the station itself. Tempus Pro is a portable telemedicine monitor used by medical teams at astronaut landings, and a flight demonstration on the station is planned. Just-in-time ultrasound guidance for non-experts has been flown. The NASA and Google Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant is a proof of concept for AI clinical support, tested on simulated scenarios, and has not flown. Each of these is a device, a single measurement, or ground support. None of them ties monitoring, personal baselines, guided triage and delayed messaging into one offline tool a non-doctor can use alone on a Mars trip. That is what CrewCare does.

CrewCare is a static web app built with HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with a hand-built chart, a service worker and local storage, hosted as a public website and in a public code repository. It runs on a phone or a computer, and in flight the same app would run on the spacecraft's onboard computer. We hope it becomes a starting point for a real crew health companion for lunar and Mars missions, and for remote clinics on Earth where a connection cannot be relied on either.
